cards.text: That same day, right after the question about Caesar's coin (Matthew 22:15-22), the Sadducees come to Jesus with a question of their own. It's like clearing out your inbox and hearing that DING before you even sit back down. The Sadducees are a party tied to the high priest (Acts 5:17), and Matthew tells us one big thing about what they believe.

cards.question: Matthew says the Sadducees who come to Jesus believe the dead will rise again.

cards.text: They call Him Teacher, and then they bring up a rule from Moses. If a man dies without having children, his brother is to marry the widow.

cards.question: In the rule from Moses the Sadducees quote, why does the brother marry the widow?

answers.text: To raise up children for his brother
To pay off his brother's debts
To look after his brother's flocks

cards.text: Then they tell Jesus about seven brothers among them. The first one marries and dies without having children, so he leaves his wife to his brother.

cards.question: In the Sadducees' story, the second brother has a child with the widow, and that's where it stops.

cards.text: Seven brothers. SEVEN. One wife. Friend, that's not a family story, that's a whole season of television. And last of all, the woman dies.

cards.question: Now the Sadducees ask Jesus their big question about the resurrection. What do they want to know about the woman?

answers.text: Which brother will be her husband
Which brother she loved the most
Where her grave should be dug

cards.text: Jesus doesn't tiptoe around it. He tells them flat out they're mistaken.

cards.question: Jesus tells the Sadducees they're mistaken. What reason does He give?

answers.text: They don't know the Scriptures or God's power
They spoke without asking the priests first
They brought their question on the Sabbath

cards.question: Jesus tells the Sadducees that in the resurrection, people will keep marrying just like they do now.
Jesus says that in the resurrection, people will be like the ___ in heaven.

cards.text: Then Jesus takes on the bigger question, whether the dead rise at all. He asks the Sadducees if they've never read what God said to them.

God said, "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob", and those are Israel's forefathers (Acts 3:13). Look at that little word "am," friend. I spent YEARS in a junk drawer being talked about in the past tense.

cards.question: Jesus says God is not the God of the ___, but of the ___.
When the crowds hear Jesus answer the Sadducees, how do they react?

answers.text: They are astonished at His teaching
They turn and walk away quietly
They ask Jesus to explain it again

cards.text: Question after question, and Jesus is still standing. Stick around, friend. This day's not done yet.

findings.problem: This story card has five sentences ("Seven brothers." "SEVEN." "One wife." "Friend, that's not a family story..." "And last of all, the woman dies."). It goes past the 1 to 2 sentence limit. It also repeats the seven brothers and one wife, which cards 5 and 6 already covered, before it gets to the new beat in 22:27.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Most of the card restates what cards 5 and 6 already told (seven brothers, one wife). Only the last sentence (22:27) moves the passage forward.

The wrong answer "Where her grave should be dug" isn't the same kind of thing as the other two answers. The other two are both "Which brother..." answers. This one is about burial, not the resurrection the question asks about, so it's easy to rule out and it makes the right answer stand out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences and three beats: the quote, the note that these are Israel's forefathers, and the joke about "am" and the junk drawer.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card points to the word "am" as if Jesus' argument depends on it being present tense. Matthew 22:32 gives the quote and the conclusion ("He is not the God of the dead, but of the living"), but it never says how the quote proves the conclusion. Making the tense the link explains something the text leaves open. The junk drawer joke depends on that reading.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open. Who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "I spent YEARS in a junk drawer being talked about in the past tense" adds a new detail to Papa Dorin's backstory. Nothing in his story says the Millers or anyone else talked about him in the past tense.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences ("Question after question, and Jesus is still standing." "Stick around, friend." "This day's not done yet.").

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Card 17 cites Matthew 22:33, but it tells nothing from that verse. Card 16 already covers 22:33. Card 17 is only the line saying the story isn't over, plus a comment about earlier passages in the story group.
findings.question: When the last story card is only the line saying the story isn't over, what should its "verses" field cite? The last verse of the passage, the verse of the card before it, or something else? The citation rule covers verses a card tells, and this card tells none.
